name: Birthday
description: Ali is Hamed's little brother and tomorrow is his birthday. Hamed wants his brother to earn his gift so he gave him a hard programming problem and told him if he can successfully solve it, he'll get him a brand new laptop. Ali is not yet a very talented programmer like Hamed and although he usually doesn't cheat but this time is an exception. It's about a brand new laptop. So he decided to secretly seek help from you. Please solve this problem for Ali. An n -vertex weighted rooted tree is given. Vertex number 1 is a root of the tree. We define d ( u , v ) as the sum of edges weights on the shortest path between vertices u and v . Specifically we define d ( u , u ) = 0 . Also let's define S ( v ) for each vertex v as a set containing all vertices u such that d (1, u ) = d (1, v ) + d ( v , u ) . Function f ( u , v ) is then defined using the following formula: The goal is to calculate f ( u , v ) for each of the q given pair of vertices. As the answer can be rather large it's enough to print it modulo 10 9 + 7 .
input_specification: In the first line of input an integer n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ), number of vertices of the tree is given. In each of the next n - 1 lines three space-separated integers a i , b i , c i ( 1 ≤ a i , b i ≤ n , 1 ≤ c i ≤ 10 9 ) are given indicating an edge between a i and b i with weight equal to c i . In the next line an integer q ( 1 ≤ q ≤ 10 5 ), number of vertex pairs, is given. In each of the next q lines two space-separated integers u i , v i ( 1 ≤ u i , v i ≤ n ) are given meaning that you must calculate f ( u i , v i ) . It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree.
output_specification: Output q lines. In the i -th line print the value of f ( u i , v i ) modulo 10 9 + 7 .
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 494D — Birthday [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
